Cardiac MRI Acquisition
Study participants were scanned on a 1.5-T MRI system
(MAGNETOM Avanto; Siemens Healthineers). Besides the
standard acquisitions, the protocol included myocardial native
and postcontrast T1 mapping and LGE imaging. T1 mapping
was
performed in basal, midventricular, and apical locations with
use of a prototype modified Look-Locker inversion
recovery T1
mapping sequence with the following image parameters: rep-
etition time msec/echo time msec, 2.6/1.1; field of view, 300 ×
256 mm
; section thickness, 8 mm; image acquisition matrix,
192 × 128; reconstruction matrix, 192 × 164; in-plane spatial
resolution, 1.56 × 1.56 mm
; bandwidth, 1085 Hz/pixel; flip
angle, 35°; and parallel imaging acceleration factor, 2. At 10–12
minutes after the administration of 0.1 mmol/kg body weight
gadobutrol (Gadavist, Bayer Healthcare), LGE images were ac-
quired in short- and long-axis orientations with the following
parameters: 2.6/1.1; field of view, 340 × 255 mm
; section thick-
ness, 8 mm; image acquisition matrix, 192 × 106; reconstruction
matrix, 192 × 144; in-plane spatial resolution, 1.77 × 1.77 mm
bandwidth, 965 Hz/pixel; and flip angle, 50°. Parallel imaging
was used with an acceleration factor of 2, and Cartesian readout
was applied. Postcontrast, T1 maps were repeated at the same
locations with a postcontrast optimized T1 sampling scheme.
CT Acquisition
All participants were scanned on a first-generation dual-source
PCD CT system (NAEOTOM Alpha; Siemens Healthineers)
with a gantry rotation time of 0.25 second in the axial plane,
at a section thickness and interval of 0.4 mm and 0.4 mm,
respectively. Tube voltage was set at 120 kV, and tube current
temporal resolution for spectral acquisitions, while provid-
ing improved spatial and contrast resolution, improved image
quality, and comprehensive spectral data with every acquisition
(16–18). In cardiac imaging, these improvements can poten-
tially translate into reduced radiation exposure, reduced beam
hardening and metal artifacts, better specificity of coronary CT
angiography for the diagnosis of coronary artery disease, and
better myocardial tissue characterization and detection of myo-
cardial ischemia (19,20).
While cardiac MRI is the clinical standard for tissue charac-
terization and evaluation of myocardial scarring, there is poten-
tial for ECV assessment by PCD CT, as shown by a recent study
with use of single- and dual-energy techniques (21). Therefore,
we hypothesized that PCD CT–based ECV mapping correlates
strongly with MRI. Due to the lack of prior validation studies
evaluating PCD CT versus reference MRI-derived
myocardial ECV quantification, we aimed to com-
pare ECV quantification by using a first-generation
PCD CT against reference MRI.
Materials and Methods
Study Participants
The
protocol
of
this
prospective,
single-center,
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability
Act–compliant study was approved by the local in-
stitutional review board at this academic medical
center, and written informed consent was obtained
from
each
participant.
Consecutive
participants
undergoing cardiac MRI for various indications
were recruited for a same-day research PCD CT
examination between July 2021 and January 2022.
All participants underwent CT immediately after
the cardiovascular MRI examination was finished
(within approximately 1 hour). Inclusion criteria
for enrollment were
being at least 18 years of age
and
having clinical indication for cardiac MRI.
Abbreviations
ECV = extracellular volume, LGE = late gadolinium enhancement,
LoA = limits of agreement, PCD = photon-counting detector
Summary
Extracellular volume quantification for myocardial tissue character-
ization obtained with a photon-counting detector CT had a strong
correlation to cardiac MRI.
